opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is that they have to be very strong engineers first. People sometimes imagine forward deployed engineering as a kind of sales or customer-success role, but in practice you're dropped into a customer's environment with messy data, legacy systems, strange constraints, and you have to actually make the model work there. That requires real technical depth: understanding how the models behave, how to evaluate them, when fine-tuning makes sense versus better prompting or retrieval, how to debug when something goes wrong.

The second thing is being pragmatic. Researchers often want to find the elegant, general solution. A good forward deployed engineer asks: what does this customer actually need, what's the simplest thing that will deliver value in a few weeks, and how do we measure that it's working? Often the bottleneck isn't the model at all. It's getting the right data, defining the task properly, or building a good evaluation set with the customer's domain experts.

Third, communication. You're the bridge between the customer and the science team. You need to explain to a customer what the model can and can't do without overselling, and you need to bring back very concrete feedback to the research side, like "the model consistently fails on this kind of document" or "this use case needs much better function calling." That feedback loop is extremely valuable for us, because it tells us what to prioritize in the next model.

And finally, ownership. The best people treat the customer's problem as their own. They don't stop at a demo; they stay until it's in production and people are actually using it. That mindset is rare, and it's what makes the difference.

r001.rationale: The response calls for strong engineering and practical model expertise, and contrasts FDE pragmatism with researchers’ preference for elegant general solutions. It does not clearly say that extensive research expertise is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: The response mentions technical depth and communication with the science team, but does not characterize the required skill set as similar to research.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when we started hiring for this at Mistral, I was skeptical of the whole concept. "Forward deployed engineer" sounded like a consulting title dressed up in startup language. But working with enterprises in Europe changed my mind, because the gap between what the model can do in a benchmark and what it does inside a bank's document pipeline is enormous, and someone has to live in that gap.

So the first thing I look for is that the person is actually a strong engineer. Not a solutions person who can demo things, but someone who can read our inference code, understand why latency spikes on long contexts, and fix it or at least diagnose it precisely enough that the research team doesn't waste a week. The best ones I've seen could have been on the core team. They chose to be closer to customers.

The second thing is a kind of humility about the problem. When you come from research, you tend to think the model is the interesting part. On a deployment, the model is maybe twenty percent of it. The rest is data that is a mess, permissions, retrieval that returns the wrong chunks, evaluations that nobody has written. A good FDE is excited by that, not annoyed by it. They treat the customer's problem as the real problem, not as an obstacle between them and the model.

Third, and this is the one that is hardest to interview for, they have to be able to translate in both directions. They go to the customer and say, no, fine-tuning won't solve this, here is what will. And they come back to us and say, here is a failure mode you have never seen because you don't have this kind of data. Several things we fixed in training came from FDEs noticing patterns across three or four customers. That feedback loop is actually why I ended up believing in the role. If it's just delivery, you don't need it. If it's a sensor on reality, it's one of the most valuable positions in the company.

And then there's temperament. You are often alone, on-site, with people who are skeptical, and things break at the worst moment. You need someone who stays calm, says "I don't know yet, give me two hours," and then actually comes back with an answer.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes strong engineering skill and customer deployment work, but it does not distinguish practical model expertise from extensive research expertise or say that research expertise is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It says the strongest FDEs could have been on the core team and should understand inference code and diagnose model behavior, conveying a skill level similar to research or core engineering.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is being able to understand what the customer is actually trying to do. They might come to you asking for a particular model or a particular feature, but you need to take a step back and understand the problem. What would make this useful for them? How would you measure whether it works?

Then you need enough technical depth to build something and iterate quickly. You’re dealing with real data, existing systems, and constraints that aren’t always clear at the beginning. So you need to be comfortable with that ambiguity, but also willing to tell the customer when an approach isn’t going to work.

And the communication goes both ways. You’re helping the customer use the technology, but you’re also bringing what you learn back to the team. A good forward deployed engineer can distinguish a very specific customer request from a problem that many customers are going to have.

r001.rationale: The response mentions technical depth and building quickly, but does not distinguish practical model expertise from extensive research expertise or say the latter is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize forward deployed engineering as requiring a skill set similar to research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s someone who can understand what the customer is actually trying to do, which is not always the same as what they’re asking for. You need to be a strong engineer, but you also need to ask good questions and be comfortable working on a problem that isn’t well defined yet.

And then you need to be pragmatic. Sometimes the right solution involves a better model; sometimes it’s changing the workflow or building a very simple integration. The important thing is to take ownership of the outcome, get something working, and learn from how people actually use it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a strong engineer may choose a better model, but does not distinguish practical model expertise from extensive research expertise or say research expertise is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes engineering, customer discovery, and pragmatism but does not characterize the skill set as similar to research.
